opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think this is a genuinely important question, and I don't want to sugarcoat it. There is a real asymmetry now. If you want to train a model at the scale of GPT-3 or GPT-4, you need compute budgets in the tens or hundreds of millions of dollars, large engineering teams, and data pipelines that no university department can match. So academia simply cannot compete head-on in that particular race, and I think it would be foolish to try.

But I don't see this as a crisis so much as a call to be smarter about what academia does best. Historically, universities have rarely been where the largest-scale engineering happens. Physicists don't build particle accelerators in their department basements; there are national labs and consortia. And yet academic physics is thriving. The question is what the right division of labor is.

Academia's comparative advantage is in ideas that are not yet fashionable, in long-horizon questions, and in training the next generation of researchers. Many of the things that turned out to matter, convolutional networks, backpropagation, reinforcement learning, a lot of the foundations of computer vision, were developed in academic settings at small scale, long before anyone knew they would pay off. Scaling is a powerful lever, but it's a lever you apply to an idea, and the ideas still have to come from somewhere.

I'd also point out that there's a lot of science to be done on these large models without training them from scratch. Understanding what they actually learn, where they fail, how they generalize, how to make them more sample efficient: these are questions academics are well placed to ask, especially when models or weights are made available. And there are domains, like embodied intelligence and robotics, which is something I care about a great deal, where it's not at all clear that scaling text is the answer. A child learns about the physical world through interaction, through manipulation and locomotion, not by reading the internet. Those problems are wide open, and they don't necessarily require a GPT-4-sized budget to make progress.

Now, I do think the relationship has to be healthy for this to work. Many of us, myself included, have had dual affiliations, spending time in industry labs while keeping a foot in academia. That cross-pollination is valuable. Industry gets access to people who are thinking about fundamental questions, and academics get exposure to problems and resources at scale. I would also like to see more public investment in shared compute, something like national research clouds, so that academic groups can at least run meaningful experiments at intermediate scale.

The danger I'd watch for is a monoculture, where everyone, in industry and academia alike, is chasing the same approach because that's where the attention and the money are. Science advances when people explore different directions. So if academia can preserve that diversity of ideas, while industry pushes the frontier of scale, I think the two can be quite complementary rather than one making the other obsolete.

r001.rationale: The candidate says academia and industry can be “quite complementary,” describing academia’s role in foundational ideas and diverse research and industry’s role in scaling models.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, let me start by saying this is not a new situation. Historically, there have been many fields where the biggest instruments were not in universities. Think about particle physics. The accelerators are at CERN or at Fermilab, and yet there's a lot of very good particle physics done in universities. Astronomy is another one. The big telescopes are shared facilities, and university astronomers get time on them. So the idea that the frontier experimental apparatus is somewhere else, and academics still contribute, is not unusual. We in computer science have been spoiled, because for decades a graduate student with a workstation could do the best work in the world. That era, for this particular slice of AI, is over, and I think we should just be honest about it rather than pretend otherwise.

Now, what does that mean for what academics should do? I'd say a few things. First, understanding. Industry is very good at building and scaling, but it's not necessarily incentivized to deeply understand why things work, to characterize failure modes, to do the careful science. Academics can take the models that exist, even through APIs, and study them. That's legitimate science. Second, there's the question of what comes next. The transformer did not come from scaling. It came from an idea. And ideas are cheap in terms of compute. If you believe, as I do, that current approaches are not the final word, that there are things these systems don't do well, in perception, in embodiment, in sample efficiency, in continual learning, then the place to work on the next idea is exactly where you aren't tied to the current paradigm by a large investment in it. Universities are good at that.

Third, I'd point out that the most important product of a university is not papers, it's people. Almost everybody at OpenAI, at DeepMind, at Google, was trained in a university. So the health of academic AI research matters to industry even on purely selfish grounds, and I think the enlightened companies understand this, which is why you see the compute donations, the shared models, the joint appointments.

I'd also say there's a specific thing I care about, which is robotics and embodied intelligence. There, the frontier is not yet compute-bound in the same way, because we don't have the data. The internet doesn't contain the data you need for a robot to learn to manipulate objects. So you still have a regime where clever ideas about how to collect data, how to simulate, how to transfer, matter more than having ten thousand GPUs. And that's a space where academic labs are, frankly, still very competitive.

So my overall attitude is not pessimistic. I think there's a division of labor emerging, and we should embrace it, while also pushing, as a community, for public compute resources so that the gap doesn't become so large that it distorts the whole field.

r001.rationale: The response describes a division of labor: industry builds and scales models, while academics study them, pursue new ideas, and contribute in areas such as robotics. It says this division should be embraced, clearly presenting the two as complementary.

astra-6.text:
I think we should distinguish between doing research on AI and training the largest possible model. Those are not the same activity. Clearly, industry has an enormous advantage in compute, data, and the engineering infrastructure needed to train something like GPT-3 or GPT-4. An academic laboratory cannot compete on those terms.

But that doesn't mean that all the important ideas will come from industry. In academia, we can ask questions that don't have an immediate commercial payoff. What are these systems actually learning? What are they missing? Can we find ways of learning that require much less data? Those are research questions, and simply making a model bigger doesn't settle them.

So I see complementary roles. Industry can build systems at scale, and those systems give us new phenomena to study. Universities can explore alternatives, examine the limitations, and train people who move between the two worlds. Access matters, of course: if researchers cannot examine these systems, it becomes harder to study them scientifically. But I wouldn't define the academic research agenda as trying to build a smaller version of whatever industry built last year.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly describes academia and industry as having complementary roles: industry builds systems at scale, while universities study them, explore alternatives, and examine limitations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there is a natural division of labor. Industry has the resources to train these very large models, and that is valuable. But academic research should not be judged by whether we can train a slightly bigger version of the same model. Our job is to ask questions, to challenge assumptions, and to explore directions whose payoff may be uncertain or far away.

For example, what does it take for a system to learn from much less data? How should learning connect to perception and action? Scaling up one approach does not settle all of those questions. A university group can make progress on them without having the computational budget of a large company.

Of course, access matters. If only a few companies can study these systems closely, that limits independent scientific investigation. So we should encourage access and collaboration. But I would not conclude that academic research has become irrelevant. It means we have to choose our problems thoughtfully, rather than simply compete with industry on its most expensive benchmark.

r001.rationale: The response describes a division of labor: industry trains very large models, while academia explores questions that do not require the same resources. It also endorses access and collaboration, presenting the roles as complementary.
